backups.overview: The Temple is the dramatic granite tower guarding the eastern edge of the Core Enchantments, rising above Prusik Pass and Tamarack Meadows in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. First climbed by Fred Beckey in 1942, its standard route follows blocky, mostly class 3-4 terrain up the peak's south side to a short, exposed 5.3-5.6 slab crux just below the summit block, protected only by a single bolt. It's commonly linked with neighboring High Priest and Prusik Peak on the same trip, but the remote, all-off-trail approach through Temple Canyon makes it a serious full-day objective even before the climbing starts.
backups.beta: Parties approach via the Snow Lakes Trail into the Core Enchantments basin, then leave the trail to ascend talus and granite buttresses on Temple's south side. The line climbs mostly class 3-4 terrain - slabs, ledges, and blocky ribs - with exposure increasing near the top, finishing with a short low-5th-class (5.3-5.6) section through a ramp/notch onto the small, airy summit. A helmet and a light rack are commonly carried for the final moves; most parties downclimb or make one or two short rappels to retreat.
backups.turnaround: Given the roughly 16-mile, 7,000+ ft round trip, set a firm turnaround time — parties have reported 12-14+ hour car-to-car days. Don't start the technical crux later than early-to-mid afternoon so you aren't descending the loose rock and rappels in the dark.
backups.rappels: 1-2 raps (a single 60m rope reaches the ground/ledge from the summit per some parties; others rappel in two stages with 30m ropes)
backups.face: West side of the summit tower (documented as the West Side route; the only detailed line to the true summit on record)
backups.permit: Enchantment permit area: overnight stays May 15-Oct 31 require a quota permit (Recreation.gov advance lottery); day trips need the free self-issued day-use permit at the trailhead.
backups.descent: Reverse the south ridge scramble back toward Prusik Pass and the Core basin.

backups.detailed_rack: No full rack is required for the scramble. A short rope and a few slings are useful to protect or hand-line the exposed steps, and an ice axe is worth carrying early in the season for snow.
pro_tips: Many parties link The Temple with High Priest and/or Prusik Peak on the same trip since all three share the Prusik Pass/Tamarack Meadows approach.
The true summit block is reportedly distinct from what some older USGS quads mark — confirm you're on the actual high point before setting up the rappel.
Descending directly toward Temple Lake instead of reversing to Prusik Pass is faster but crosses looser, steeper terrain — downclimb carefully or rope up.
Rock shoes make the 5.3-5.6 summit-block crux considerably easier — worth carrying even though most of the route is done in approach shoes/boots.
watch_out: The crux slab move is protected by only one old bolt — inspect it before weighting and back it up with gear if you can.
Loose blocks litter the ridge and gully below the summit — helmets on, and stay alert to parties above or below.
This is a very long day even for fit parties (14+ hours car-to-car has been reported) — start pre-dawn and set a firm turnaround time.
backups.pro_needs: The standard line is largely unprotected scrambling, with the option to sling horns or place the occasional small piece on the most exposed steps. Comfort on exposed fourth-class terrain is the key requirement rather than a large rack.
backups.approach: From the Snow Lakes Trailhead at the end of Icicle Creek Road (about 4.3 mi from US-2, ~1,300 ft elevation), cross Icicle Creek on the trail bridge and begin the long, switchbacking climb up open, sun-baked slabs on Snow Lakes Trail No. 1553 — this lower stretch is notoriously hot with almost no shade, so carry more water than feels necessary for the first few miles. The grade eases as the trail enters the hanging valley and reaches Nada Lake at roughly 5.5-5.6 miles (~5,000 ft), banking most of the day's approach mileage but only a bit over half the total gain. Follow the trail/use path along the lake's west shore past scattered campsites to Nada Creek near the lake's upper end — a boulder-hop in normal summer flow, but a genuine ford in early-season high water. Immediately past the creek, leave the maintained trail: climb a cairned climbers' path staying along the south edge of a broad talus field toward the notch that opens into Temple Canyon. Where the talus narrows to roughly 75 ft, work right onto a class 2-3 ledge system that skirts a waterfall, then continue up slabs into scattered trees. A steep, loose dirt-and-rock climbers' path then leads into Temple Canyon proper, staying near the stream (the last reliable water before the summit block) as it steepens toward the canyon head. Near the top, scramble up and left onto the broad, larch-dotted plateau of Tamarack Meadows (~6,600 ft), cross another talus/boulder field above treeline, and follow a final sandy ramp under an overhang to the base of the South Ridge's technical section. Figure roughly 8 miles and ~7,000 ft one-way from the trailhead to the 8,295 ft summit — about 16-16.5 miles round trip, a very long car-to-car day if not camping at Nada Lake or in the canyon. Hazards: sustained sun exposure with no shade on the lower switchbacks, an unbridged Nada Creek crossing that gets serious with early-season snowmelt, faint cairn-dependent route-finding above Nada Lake, loose talus and scree throughout Temple Canyon, and lingering snow on north-facing ledges into early summer.
backups.descent_text: Because the South Ridge is cliffed-out on multiple sides, parties descend by downclimbing and rappelling the same south-side line used on the ascent rather than walking off. From the summit block, the first rappel drops off a fixed station just below the top — parties describe a single old, not-fully-confidence-inspiring bolt/pin anchor here, so back it up with a cam or nut if you have any doubt — down past the 5.3-5.6 friction slab crux to a ledge. From there, most parties make one further rappel through a band of loose rock and boulders to a notch where the anchor is natural: a sling around a large wedged chockstone (some parties have refreshed this with a new sling and rap ring). A single 60m rope rappelled doubled (~30m per pitch) is generally sufficient, but at least one party found the rope only just reached the next station, so treat 60m as a minimum, knot your rope ends, and expect some parties to break the descent into three shorter rappels instead of two depending on the exact gully line and rope length carried. After the last rappel, downclimb and plunge-step the loose gully below the rockfall zone back onto the ascent talus, then retrace the approach through Temple Canyon, Tamarack Meadows, and the climbers' path back to Nada Lake and the Snow Lakes Trail. Wear a helmet throughout the descent — the gully channels loose rock kicked down by parties above.
backups.bail: Retreat is reasonable at most points by reversing the scramble, though the exposed fourth-class steps demand care on the downclimb. A short rope helps protect a retreat if the weather turns on the upper ridge.

pitch_detail.notes: ~70 ft up a friction face directly toward the summit, protected by one bolt; crux of the route.
Ledge system leads left and up to a belay on a wide, level block just below/north of the true summit, then a short crack leads to the top.

itinerary.cal: Enchantments Core Zone overnight permits are lottery-based (applications open in Feb); without one, most parties either do the ~16-mile car-to-car single push or camp outside the Core Zone near Nada Lake/Snow Lakes instead of at Temple Canyon.

This leg alone is roughly as long and steep as many peaks' entire round trip.

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day/2-night backpack is the common way to climb The Temple: roughly 19-20 miles and ~7,000 ft gain round trip, with day 2 as the technical summit day (~8 hrs, class 4/low-5th crux, rappel descent). Strong parties without an Enchantments overnight permit instead push the whole thing car-to-car in one very long day (documented at 16.5 mi / ~7,000 ft, ~14-16 hrs, 4:30 AM start).

access.fees: Overnight Enchantment permits cost $5.00 per person per day (May 15-Oct 31) plus a $6.00 non-refundable lottery application fee; day use has no permit fee.
access.notes: 2026 lottery application window Feb 15–Mar 1 (results after Mar 17, accept/pay by Mar 31). ~25% of overnight slots also released as a walk-up daily lottery the day before entry. Season requiring the overnight permit: May 15–Oct 31. A single-day ascent with no camp inside the boundary never needs the lottery.
access.rules: Wilderness group size is limited (8 people); no campfires are allowed above roughly 6,000 ft / within the Core Enchantment Zone; camp only in designated or already-established durable sites.
access.permit: Day trips only need a free self-issue day-use permit, available at the Snow Lakes Trailhead. Overnight camping anywhere within the Enchantment Permit Area (including the Temple Canyon/Tamarack Meadows/Prusik Pass approach) requires a reserved overnight permit May 15-Oct 31, allocated through the Recreation.gov Enchantments lottery — a February advance lottery plus a daily geofence lottery you apply for one day ahead for the remainder of the season.
access.closures: Icicle Creek Road and the Snow Lakes Trailhead have been subject to wildfire-related closures in dry summers — check current Wenatchee River Ranger District alerts before driving in.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District (Leavenworth); route lies within the Alpine Lakes Wilderness and the Enchantment Permit Area.

access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Stuart Lake, Eightmile, and Snow Lakes trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (overnight permit holders get a covering parking pass instead).
access.passRequired: A Northwest Forest Pass (or America the Beautiful interagency pass) is required to park at the Snow Lakes Trailhead.

climate.fall: Larch season (late Sept-early Oct) draws heavy hiker traffic to the basin; early snow/ice possible by October.
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack persists into June-July on Aasgard Pass and upper basin approaches.
climate.summer: Prime climbing window (Jul-Sep); can still be hot and exposed with limited shade in the granite basin.
climate.winter: Deep snow and avalanche terrain; not a standard climbing season for this route.
climate.typical: A short climbing season: heavy Cascade snowpack lingers in the north-facing approach gullies and shaded ledges into July, while summers are typically dry under Pacific high-pressure systems; afternoon thunderstorms are possible July-August.

bySeason.fall: Stable weather can continue into September and even early October, but overnight freezes and early snow can arrive quickly at this elevation, and days shorten fast.
bySeason.spring: Deep snow and avalanche hazard on the approach through Temple Canyon; not a typical climbing season.
bySeason.summer: Prime season (July-September); the trail and talus approach are usually mostly snow-free by mid-to-late July in an average year, but watch for afternoon thunderstorms.
bySeason.winter: Not a viable climbing season — deep snow and avalanche terrain throughout the approach.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC does not directly forecast the Enchantments; check the NOAA point forecast for the Snow Lakes/Enchantments area (nearest broader avalanche/weather context comes from the Stevens Pass/Central Cascades zone).

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is unreliable to nonexistent through most of the Enchantments basin. The Chelan County Sheriff's Office runs frequent summer SAR missions into the Colchuck Lake/Enchantments zone for injured, exhausted, or disoriented hikers and climbers — given the remoteness and very long approach, carry a satellite messenger or PLB.
emergency.rangerStation: Wenatchee River Ranger District, Leavenworth, WA (Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest)
emergency.nearestHospital: Cascade Medical Center, Leavenworth, WA — 24-hour emergency department and ambulance service.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Chelan County Sheriff's Office — call 911; backcountry search and rescue is coordinated through the Chelan County Sheriff's Office Search and Rescue unit (with Chelan County Mountain Rescue volunteers).

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekend and holiday periods July-September when Enchantments core-zone permit holders are camped near Prusik Pass/the Core and add it as a side scramble; parties often combine it with The High Priest via a low traverse the same day.
crowds.estimatePerSeason: No precise count is known; likely low-to-moderate — a few to several dozen parties per season. The Temple sits inside the heavily-trafficked Enchantments core zone (permit-limited but reportedly crowded on peak weekends), yet the South Ridge itself is a side objective from camp, far less climbed than Prusik Peak or the standard Enchantments thru-hike route.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Multi-day backpacking fitness — the approach to a Prusik Pass/Core camp involves significant mileage and ~4,000+ ft of elevation gain (via Snow Lakes or Colchuck/Aasgard Pass) before the summit day itself.
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight/multi-day pack (roughly 30-40 lb) to reach camp, then a light summit pack for the ridge itself.

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long — typically 1-2 days to establish a camp near Prusik Pass or in the Core via Snow Lakes or Colchuck/Aasgard Pass, then several hours round-trip for the ridge from camp.

partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced scrambler comfortable soloing sustained Class 3-4 terrain with real exposure; alpine scrambling background rather than a first-timer route, consistent with the exposed fourth-class steps and route-finding-to-the-true-summit hazards.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July through October, with July-August the most reliable window for snow-free rock.

July.reason: Season typically opens as snow clears from the approach and ridge; matches start of best season.

August.reason: Driest, most stable rock and weather of the season, though afternoon thunderstorms remain a known hazard.

October.reason: Still within the best-season, but cold temps, shorter daylight, and potential early snowfall increase risk on exposed fourth-class terrain.

September.reason: Stable, cooler weather with fewer thunderstorms, but shorter days and possible early-season snow late in the month.

weather.typical: High-alpine Cascades summer pattern — generally clear, settled mornings with potential for rapid afternoon buildup at this exposed 8,295 ft summit.
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are a known and common hazard, especially July-August; exposed summit terrain compounds lightning risk.

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Significant fall exposure on the fourth-class steps and loose-rock sections of the ridge; a slip in the exposed sections would likely result in a serious long fall rather than a minor tumble, so rope/protection judgment on the 4th-class crux matters even though the route is typically climbed unroped.

avalanche.zone: N/A - dry summer/fall scrambling route climbed outside NWAC's active winter/spring forecast season; the Enchantments/Stuart Range area falls loosely under NWAC's Stevens Pass zone in winter, but that has no bearing on this route's July-October climbing window.

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel; this is a granite ridge scramble.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Snow Lakes Trailhead at the end of Icicle Creek Road (about 4.3 mi from US-2, ~1,300 ft elevation)

backups.corrections: Route naming conflict: this line is documented under the name 'West Side' by The Mountaineers (mountaineers.org), while the DB entry (and this research) uses 'South Ridge' as given — these very likely refer to the same standard/easiest line to The Temple's summit (the peak's original 1942 Beckey line), but no source was found that independently confirms a distinctly-named 'South Ridge' route separate from the Mountaineers' 'West Side' description; flagging so this can be verified against a guidebook (e.g. Beckey's Cascade Alpine Guide) if the name matters. Grade also varies by source: Mountaineers.org and a 2015 Cascadeclimbers trip report both describe a 5.6 crux move on the friction slab, while Wikipedia (derived from Peakbagger-style summary) states the 'easiest route' is class 5.3 — both are reported here since neither could be ruled out as more authoritative.

approach_variants.name: Snow Lakes trail, Nada Lake and Temple Canyon
approach_variants.notes: A very long day from the road even for fit parties. The lower Snow Lakes trail switchbacks up open, sun-baked slabs with almost no shade, so carry more water than feels sensible; the grade eases into the hanging valley at Nada Lake around five and a half miles. Follow the west shore to the creek at the lake's upper end, a boulder-hop in normal flow and a genuine ford in early-season melt, and leave the maintained trail immediately past it. A cairned climbers' path runs along the south edge of a broad talus field toward the notch into Temple Canyon; where the talus narrows to roughly seventy-five feet, work right onto a ledge system that skirts a waterfall, then up slabs into scattered trees. A steep, loose path leads into the canyon proper — stay near the stream, which is the last reliable water below the summit block.
approach_variants.season: July to early October; axe in June
hazards: Loose, blocky rock on the approach ledges and along the ridge, with large poised blocks near the summit block
A rockfall zone directly below the start of the technical ground — do not linger under it
Exposed class 4 scrambling and a short low-fifth-class crux protected by a single aged bolt
Faint, cairn-dependent route-finding above Nada Lake
Lingering snow on north-facing ledges and in the gullies into early summer
Old rappel anchors and slings that periodically need replacing — carry spare webbing
approach_variants.baseFinding: Near the head of Temple Canyon, scramble up and left onto the broad, larch-dotted plateau at about 6,600 ft; this is where the tower first shows itself properly, and from the base of the ridge it is unmistakable. Cross the talus and boulder field above treeline, with giant blocks scattered below the north end of the towers and more strewn along the ridgeline. The start of the technical ground is a single specific feature: a sandy ramp running up beneath an overhang, at the far right-hand end of the base of the ridge. Nothing else there looks like it. The classic error is to veer right toward the neighbouring buttresses on the assumption that the ramp can be bypassed — it cannot, and parties that try end up reversing to the ramp. The ground under the ramp is the fall line for anything dislodged above, so get on it and move rather than racking up beneath it.

climbing_route.label: Sandy ramp under the overhang
climbing_route.notes: The technical climbing starts where the approach ends, at a sandy ramp running up beneath an overhang toward the right side of the buttress. This is scrambling rather than climbing, but it is sandy over rock and is the start of the fall line for anything dislodged above — the ground below this point is described as a rockfall zone and parties downclimb or rappel out of it rather than lingering.

climbing_route.label: Exposed ridge below the summit block
climbing_route.notes: Above the ramp the line follows the ridge with several exposed fourth-class moves leading to the base of the summit block. The recurring hazard reported here is loose rock: large, poised blocks are scattered along the ridgeline, so test holds and keep the party out of each other's fall line. Zig-zagging is characteristic of the route, and long slings are recommended to control rope drag when it is climbed on a rope.

climbing_route.label: Summit-block crux
climbing_route.notes: The crux is a short low-fifth-class sequence on the summit block, graded anywhere from 5.3 to 5.6. The published sequence reaches well out left to a flake and uses the narrow ledge above it as a handhold. Accounts of the summit block also record a small, old and visibly rusty bolt low on a friction slab with essentially no other gear available on that section, so the protection is thin and the bolt should not be trusted as a running belay. Sticky rubber is repeatedly recommended for this bit. Small cams to about 2 inches plus stoppers is the reported rack.

climbing_route.label: Thin ramp to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Above the crux a thin ramp trends east and reaches the roomy summit with one last fourth-class move. Descent is by rappelling the route rather than by any walk-off: three rappels with a single 60 m rope is the reported configuration — one from the end of the technical climbing to a bolted belay ledge, one from chains down the face trending skier's left which just barely reaches third-class ground, and one from a large boulder wrapped in webbing down to the talus. Carry spare webbing; the anchors are old and the slings periodically need replacing.

backups.overview: Abernathy Peak is the high point of Abernathy Ridge, between the Twisp River and Wolf Creek drainages in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. The more heavily traveled standard route climbs from Scatter Lake on the south side (class 2); the North Ridge described here is a quieter, more sustained class 2-3 alternative reached from Wolf Creek and Gardner Meadows to the north, climbing past an old mining camp at a small tarn and up a spur ridge onto the crest before scrambling to the summit.
backups.beta: Rather than the popular Scatter Lake approach, this line reaches Abernathy from Gardner Meadows to the north, climbing a spur ridge from a small tarn onto the main north ridge, then scrambling the crest — weaving around or over gendarmes — to the top. Route-finding is loose and 'pick-your-own-adventure' in spots; parties report it as noticeably harder and slower than the standard route.
backups.turnaround: Loose rock, exposed class 3-4 steps, and a long, largely trail-less descent mean parties should set a firm turnaround time that leaves ample daylight for a slower-than-expected reverse scramble, especially in poor visibility or if unfamiliar with route-finding on open ridges.

backups.permit: No wilderness permit is required to hike or camp in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. No parking pass is needed at the Wolf Creek trailhead.

backups.detailed_rack: No roped rock rack is carried on this route. Cross-referenced trip reports consistently describe the non-standard North Ridge (via the Wolf Creek/Gardner Meadows trail and an old, largely-vanished mine boot path) as an unroped Class 2-3 scramble: talus and scree to Gardner Meadows, then an unmaintained path/cairns to a tarn and a spur ridge onto the crest, then a 'pick-your-own-adventure' scramble along the ridge crest with 'a few class 3 moves' on a spur ridge. No party describes placing cams, nuts, or using a rope.

backups.pro_needs: None placed — this is unprotected scrambling, not protected rock climbing. Hazard is loose rock/footing (talus, scree, old mining debris) rather than lack of gear placements; a helmet is the relevant safety item, not a rack.
backups.approach: Start at the Wolf Creek Trailhead (about 3,000 ft), reached from Winthrop by Twin Lakes Road, Wolf Creek Road and a gravel Forest Service road to its end. Wolf Creek Trail #527 drops a couple of hundred feet to the creek and then rolls up the valley through forest heavily burned in 2021, entering the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness early on; it is a long, up-and-down walk of about 10 miles to Gardner Meadows at the end of the trail, where most parties camp. From one of the last campsites, a faint path crosses Wolf Creek and continues up the far side toward Abernathy Lake; it is an old, abandoned trail that disappears in the old burn, so the rest is off-trail. Stay high above Abernathy Lake rather than dropping to it, and make a rising traverse into the upper basin with a small tarn, where the remains of an old cabin and mining equipment mark the old mining camp; a stream just below the tarn is the last reliable water. From the tarn, climb the spur ridge rising to the main north ridge, which has a few exposed class 3 moves, then follow a short boot path along the crest past more mining remains. The path fades past the mine, and the rest is class 2-3 scrambling on boulders and scree to the summit. The upper slopes face south and are normally snow-free from about early July; earlier, firm snow can make the loose talus easier at the cost of carrying an axe.
backups.descent_text: Abernathy Peak's North Ridge is a scramble, not a technical roped climb, and no fixed rappel anchors exist on this route — descend by reversing the ascent line. From the summit, downclimb/scramble the class 3 ridge crest north back toward the top of the spur ridge (the route's crux terrain, with a couple of noticeably 'intense' exposed spots — face in and downclimb deliberately here, since the same loose, eroded rock that's manageable going up is more consequential coming down). From there, most parties drop down the scree slope toward the tarn with the old mining camp rather than reversing the spur ridge; an old path leaves the crest and descends to the upper lake. From the tarn, retrace the rough off-trail line past Abernathy Lake back to Gardner Meadows and follow the Wolf Creek Trail out to the trailhead. This is a 0-rappel walk-off/downclimb in normal summer conditions — no rope, rack, or anchors needed. Parties who ascended on firm early-season snow should be ready to descend the upper slopes via glissade or a controlled snow descent with an ice axe instead of scree, and should watch for rockfall from parties above given the generally loose rock on this route.
backups.bail: Retreat down the ridge to the approach.

pitch_detail.notes: Ridge-crest scramble from the top of the spur ridge to the summit, weaving around or over gendarmes; loose rock and unmarked route-finding.

itinerary.cal: The ridge and the slopes above the tarn can hold snow into early summer; most parties climb it July-October.

approach_variants.name: Gardner Meadows to the north ridge
approach_variants.notes: This is the side every recorded ascent of the north ridge has come from. Maps show an old trail running west from Gardner Meadows toward a mine at a small tarn on the peak's northeast side, but there is very little evidence of it leaving the meadows and it is effectively abandoned: parties bushwhack along its rough line, picking up occasional cairns and cut logs, and the tread only firms up nearer the tarn. Expect the trail to peter out past the campsites and the going to become a matter of climbing over, around and under downed timber. Keep above the lake below the ridge rather than dropping to it. The north side can also be entered from the North Creek valley on the far side of the range, but that way is undescribed, so the marks below are written for this approach rather than that one.
approach_variants.season: The upper slopes face south and are normally clear from about early July. Earlier in the season, firmer snow makes the loose upper talus easier to travel at the cost of carrying an axe and crampons.
hazards: The mapped trail is abandoned and largely invisible leaving the meadows
Heavy deadfall low down, with long stretches of climbing over and under log jams
No maintained tread and no reliable cairns; the boot path that does exist is short and intermittent
Loose class 2 and 3 boulders and scree on the crest, with route choice left entirely to the party
Water is limited to the stream near the tarn — nothing dependable above it
approach_variants.baseFinding: The dried-up tarn with cabin remnants is the proof, and the old mine on the crest confirms it. Working west from the meadows, the tread becomes distinct only as you near a small dried-up tarn on the peak's northeast side, known to some as Nasty Pond. Beside it are the remnants of a small cabin and an old pot sitting on a fire pit. That wreckage is the marker — there is no sign, no cairn at the turn, and no maintained trail — and a good stream just below it is the last reliable water. From the tarn, climb the spur ridge rising directly to the main north ridge; expect a few class 3 moves on it. Once on the crest you pick up a short stretch of boot path running through old mining evidence, with metal cables and other equipment lying on the rocks, and that hardware is the confirmation you are on the historic line rather than a game trail. The path disappears past the mine and the rest is pick-your-own-line class 2 and 3 through boulders and scree to the top. Coming down, the scree slope back to the pond is generally preferred over reversing the spur ridge.

backups.overview: One of the most celebrated alpine rock climbs in the Cascades and one of the original Fifty Classic Climbs of North America, capped by the dramatic Great Gendarme. The upper (original) North Ridge was first climbed by John Rupley and Don Claunch (later Don Gordon) in 1956 (they bypassed the Gendarme); the Gendarme itself was first climbed directly by James Wickwire and Fred Stanley in 1964. About 11 pitches of low-to-mid 5th class "bomber rock" lead from the notch above the Stuart Glacier to the base of the Gendarme, followed by two crux 5.9 pitches (a steep lieback into a strenuous offwidth), then several more pitches of 4th/low-5th class to the summit — roughly 18 pitches and 3,000 ft total.
backups.beta: Considered one of the finest alpine rock climbs in the Cascades and one of the '50 Classic Climbs of North America.' The lower ~11 pitches are exposed but moderate (low/mid 5th, one 5.7 move); the Gendarme supplies the technical crux.
backups.turnaround: Set a turnaround based on reaching the Great Gendarme by early afternoon; retreating from above it is slow and serious.
backups.rappels: None on the standard descent — the Cascadian Couloir is a walk-off/downclimb. The only rappel on the route is optional and on the way up: a ~75 ft rappel off the right side of the ridge below the Great Gendarme, from an established fixed sling (not bolted), used to bypass the 5.9 crux pitches. A single 60m rope doubled covers it.
backups.permit: Enchantment permit area: overnight stays May 15-Oct 31 require a quota permit (Recreation.gov advance lottery); day trips need the free self-issued day-use permit at the trailhead.
backups.comms: Cell coverage is spotty to absent on the north side of the peak; occasional signal reported from the ridge crest and summit.
backups.descent: Descend via Cascadian Couloir (south side) to Long's Pass and trail descent to Esmerelda Trailhead. Alternatively (early season), descend Sherpa Glacier to Stuart Lake Trailhead. The Cascadian Couloir descent is long and loose; pre-descent scouting of the false summit notch essential.

backups.best_season: July through September for dry rock and minimal snow on the approach. Early season adds glacier and snow complexity.
backups.approach: Primary approach is from the north via the Stuart Lake Trailhead (reached via Icicle Creek Road and FR 7601 out of Leavenworth). From the trailhead, follow the Stuart/Colchuck Lake Trail as it rolls along Mountaineer Creek through forest; at the signed junction roughly 2 miles in, stay left/straight (the Colchuck Lake fork splits right). Continue on the Mountaineer Creek/Stuart Lake trail for about another 0.2 mile, then leave the maintained trail before reaching Stuart Lake itself, cross Mountaineer Creek, and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. After roughly 2 more miles of streamside travel, climb a steep, loose talus/boulder slope to gain the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa Glacier — this valley has good bivy sites and is a common overnight stop. From the valley, angle directly up to the toe of the North Ridge, keeping the Ice Cliff Glacier on your left; the notch/base of the upper ridge sits around 8,200 ft, where a snow-filled gully (often climbed on 4th-class rock at its edge) gains the crest. All-in this is roughly 6-6.5 miles and 3,300+ ft of gain, about 4-5 hours to the base of the climbing. A well-known alternative is the southern approach via the Esmeralda/Teanaway trailhead over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, gaining the ridge from that side (~9 miles, ~4,800 ft gain, ~8 hours) — longer and higher-gain on the way in, but it sets up a much shorter car-to-car loop for parties planning to descend the Cascadian Couloir, since that descent drops back toward Ingalls Creek. Water is available at Mountaineer Creek and its south fork on the north approach, and at Ingalls Creek/seasonal snow patches near the 8,200 ft notch bivy on the south approach; above the notch there is no reliable water. Route-finding through the boulder/talus slope below Sherpa Glacier and the creek crossing (higher and faster in early season) are the main approach-specific hazards.
backups.descent_text: Nearly all parties descend via the Cascadian Couloir on the mountain's south side — this is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling required (0 rappels) under normal summer conditions. From the true summit, downclimb steep snow or scree, keeping right through sparse trees to drop into the head of the Cascadian Couloir, then follow the couloir down its full length (loose sand, scree, and rockfall-prone rock the entire way; an ice axe, and often crampons, are recommended into mid-summer for a lingering snow tongue) to the valley floor near Ingalls Creek, roughly 4,000 ft below the summit. The upper couloir splits into a confusing maze of climbers' paths and cairns — keep to the established talus path on the climber's left side around the 8,800 ft permanent snowfield; parties who drift onto the right side have run into old rappel-station remnants and much harder downclimbing. Because the North Ridge is climbed from the north (Stuart Lake/Mountaineer Creek side) while the Cascadian Couloir exits to the south (Ingalls Creek/Teanaway side), most parties face a long, tiring hike back around the mountain to a north-side vehicle — either via Longs Pass and a car shuttle, or a full trail loop back to the Stuart Lake Trailhead; parties using the southern (Esmeralda/Longs Pass) approach avoid this by parking on that side to begin with. Note: some parties opt for a short, optional ~75 ft rappel off the right side of the ridge below the Great Gendarme (using an established, well-traveled sling/fixed anchor, not bolted) to bypass the crux 5.9 pitches during the ascent — this is a mid-route bypass rappel, not part of the standard descent, and is not counted in the rappel total below. A single 60m rope doubled (or a single-strand lower) is sufficient for it.
backups.bail: Low on the ridge you can reverse/rappel to the glacier and retreat. Above the Great Gendarme, bailing requires committing rappels — most parties continue to the summit and descend the Cascadian.

approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FR 7601 (Eightmile Road) out of Leavenworth and walk the Stuart Lake Trail up Mountaineer Creek. At the signed split roughly two miles along, ignore the Colchuck Lake branch on the right and carry straight on. A short distance further you leave maintained tread altogether, well before Stuart Lake, ford Mountaineer Creek and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. Late in the season there is a cairned climbers' path through much of this; early in the season there is not, and the creek runs hard.

Above the streamside travel a steep, unstable talus and boulder slope lifts you into the hanging basin under Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa Glacier. This basin holds the usual bivies. From it you angle up onto the glacier bench beneath the ridge.

This is the shorter, lower-gain way in and it puts you at the toe with the most in the tank, but it commits you to a car shuttle: the standard descent is the Cascadian Couloir, which spills out on the far side of the range at Ingalls Creek. Parties report the shuttle drive between the two trailheads costing several hours round trip. In June and early July the Sherpa Glacier is a reasonable way back down to this side and removes the shuttle problem — later in the summer it is not.

There is running snowmelt near the toe of the ridge (reported around 47.48095, -120.89454); above the 8,200 ft notch there is no reliable water once the last snow patch there melts out.
approach_variants.season: Jun to mid-Jul is the sweet spot; workable through Sep
hazards: Mountaineer Creek and its south fork run high and fast in early-season melt
Loose talus and boulder slope below the Sherpa Glacier basin — poor footing, rockfall onto parties below
Serac and icefall exposure if you drift east under the Ice Cliff Glacier
No reliable water above the 8,200 ft notch once its snow patch is gone
Committing: standard descent exits on the opposite side of the range, so a shuttle or a very long walk-around is required
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are climbing the complete North Ridge, which begins at about 6,600 ft — roughly 1,500 ft of roped ground below the point where most people who say 'North Ridge' actually start. The toe is the lowest rock of the rib that separates the two glaciers: Stuart Glacier on its west side, Ice Cliff Glacier on its east. Standing at the base with the Ice Cliff Glacier and its seracs on your left and the Stuart Glacier hidden around the corner to your right, you are in the right place. If you are underneath hanging ice you have drifted too far east onto the Ice Cliff side and need to come back west to the rib's lowest rock.

The feature to not mistake for the start is the notch at 8,200 ft. That notch is obvious — a saddle in the crest with a scatter of bivy platforms and, usually, a small lingering snowfield for water — and it is where the Upper (original) North Ridge begins. It is reached by a rock gully climbed from the edge of the Stuart Glacier at about 7,700 ft, on the ridge's west flank. If you find yourself scrambling a gully up from snow toward a bivy saddle, you have skipped the lower 1,500 ft and are on the Upper route, not the Complete.

In cloud, use the glaciers rather than the rock: the toe is where the moraine/snow of the basin runs out against the first continuous rock, and the ice above and left of you belongs to the Ice Cliff Glacier. The 8,200 ft notch is above and right of that, reached only after the ridge has already risen well above the ice.

approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737), take the trail over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, then traverse east beneath the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe of the ridge.

About 2,000 ft of the day is descent, so the round trip is more work than the raw gain suggests, and parties consistently report it taking longer than planned — budget eight hours and expect route-finding on the traverse rather than tread.

The reason to accept the longer, higher approach is that it removes the shuttle entirely. The Cascadian Couloir descent drops to Ingalls Creek on this side, so a party that walked in from Esmeralda walks out to its own car. Parties who came in from the north do not.

How much snow remains on the Goat Pass traverse is the recurring gear question here: sections have been reported at around 40 degrees, and whether you need an axe and traction changes week to week through the summer. Recent photos and current reports are worth more than any fixed answer.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
Coming from Goat Pass you arrive at the ridge from below and to the west, which is the opposite side from the northern approach — so the Ice Cliff Glacier is not your handrail here, the Stuart Glacier is. Keep the Stuart Glacier snow on your left as you traverse east and stay above the big moraine mound; the toe of the Complete ridge is the first continuous rock the traverse runs into, at about 6,600 ft.

The decision point is unmissable once you know to look for it: from the edge of the Stuart Glacier at roughly 7,700 ft a rock gully leads up the ridge's west side to the notch at 8,200 ft. Taking that gully puts you on the Upper North Ridge and skips the lower 1,500 ft. Continuing the traverse past and below it, down to the lowest rock, is what starts the Complete route. In poor visibility: if the snow you are standing on is still rising to your right toward a saddle, you are too high; the toe is below, where the snow ends.

backups.name: Drilling Me Softly
hazards: Loose and sharp rock is a known issue at this recently-developed alpine sport crag.
The approach and crag sit in a remote basin with no cell coverage, so any injury means a long self-evacuation or SAR response.
backups.overview: Alpine sport climb at Sofa King Buttress in The Citidel area.
backups.beta: Fully bolted 5.10b/c sport pitch on Sofa King Buttress, positioned as the leftmost route on the wall. The line (FA party Wylie Moreshead) is known for the sheer variety of technique packed into one pitch rather than a single hard crux — 3D stemming, backstepping, flagging, a roof, laybacking, jugs, crimps and underclings. Protected by 12 bolts to chain anchors at the top; photos of the route show the crux section and a rest stance before an upper bulge.
backups.turnaround: Not a big-mountain turnaround-time objective — the real time constraint is the 20-30 minute approach through Silver Basin and weather: the approach and buttress base are exposed, so turn back on the approach if lightning or fast-moving weather threatens before you're committed to the rock.
backups.rappels: Single lower-off from chain anchors at the top.
backups.comms: No documented cell coverage in this remote, forested Silver Basin approach off NF-9070; treat the area as a dead zone and carry a satellite messenger for emergencies.
backups.descent: Lower off the chain anchor at the top of the route.

backups.detailed_rack: Fully bolted: 12 bolts to a two-bolt chain anchor. No trad gear needed.

backups.pro_needs: Sport rack only — 12 quickdraws (plus 1-2 extra for the anchor). No natural/trad protection required or possible.

backups.approach: From I-90 Exit 54 (Hyak), follow Hyak Drive onto Forest Service Road NF-9070, continuing past where the pavement ends to the junction at Ollallie Meadow where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses the road. Take the left fork of NF-9070 and follow it until the road terminates in a large turnaround just below Silver Basin. From that turnaround, it's roughly a 20-30 minute approach on foot up into Silver Basin to reach the base of The Citadel's walls, including Sofa King Buttress on the NW side of the basin's east wall. The road is not plowed and is generally only clear of snow from around July through November.
backups.descent_text: Single-pitch, fully bolted sport route with a chain lower-off anchor at the top; there is no walk-off. Clip/thread the chains and lower back to the base.
backups.bail: Single-pitch and fully bolted — retreat simply means lowering off the last bolt clipped (leave a biner/draw behind if you can't otherwise clean while lowering).

pitch_detail.notes: Sustained, technically varied bolted pitch — 3D stemming, backstepping, flagging, a roof, laybacks, jugs, crimps, underclings — 12 bolts to chain anchor; furthest-left line on the buttress.

backups.name: Hourglass Gully (Winter)
backups.fa: Jim Pritchard, Stan Jensen & Cecil Bailey (1963)
hazards: Active avalanche paths dominate the Hourglass Gully; the gully is a natural funnel for snow and debris from the upper peak
Icefall and rockfall on the right side of the Hourglass Gully are frequent; this section is the objective hazard pinch-point
Exposure on the upper East Ridge is extreme; a slip or rope failure is likely fatal; this is a serious mountaineering undertaking
Dense brush on the ridge between the lake saddle and the summit is a major objective hazard in summer; winter and spring ascents avoid this via snow
Cornices form on the summit ridge; avoid stepping on cornice edges, especially on the north side
backups.overview: A classic winter alpine ascent of Mount Index's Main Peak via a steep gully and exposed ridge, offering 1,900 feet of technical snow/ice climbing with significant avalanche and rockfall hazard.
backups.beta: Begin at Lake Serene trailhead, ascend 2,000 feet through forest to the lake (4.1 miles), then climb steeply southeast toward the summit. The Hourglass Gully presents 40-60 degree snow and ice, with a crux 60-degree pitch on the East Ridge. The gully constricts dramatically near the exit with near-vertical sections. Timing is critical; the window for this route is narrow (early March through early May). After May, melted conditions expose loose rock and create severe bushwhacking challenges.
backups.turnaround: Establish a firm turnaround time based on daylight hours and team fitness. For winter ascents starting at 2:30 AM from the car, a noon turnaround from the summit area (giving 8-10 hours for approach and climb) allows 4-6 hours for descent and the 4.1-mile trail before dark. If the turnaround time is reached before gaining the upper Hourglass Gully constriction, descend immediately. Do not attempt the technical upper gully in fading light.
backups.rappels: 2-3 raps (two 30 m ropes) from the upper gully/East Ridge down to roughly the saddle above Lake Serene; anchors are typically slung trees, horns, or pickets rather than fixed hardware.
backups.comms: Cell phone coverage in the Index/Gold Bar area is generally good (71-93% coverage depending on carrier, with T-Mobile 5G covering ~72%). However, once on the peak and in high alpine terrain, cell coverage becomes unreliable or nonexistent, especially on the ridge or in the gully. Satellite communicators (PLBs, inReach) are strongly recommended for emergencies; traditional cell phones cannot be relied upon for rescue coordination from the peak.
backups.descent: Descend via the same route. The East Ridge section is often rappelled on descent, requiring two 30-meter ropes to navigate the steep, forested terrain. Climbers typically boot-ski or downclimb the Hourglass Gully in spring snow conditions, with small wet slides common. The final descent returns via the Lake Serene trail.

wet-snow avalanche/sluffing inside the confined gully
dense brush and loose rock on the East Ridge approach

backups.detailed_rack: Two 30-meter ropes (single-rope rappels, doubled for security), dynamic belay anchors or pickets at rap stations. Ice axe (technical climbing tool essential for step-cutting and self-arrest). Crampons (rigid or semi-rigid, microspikes insufficient). Rock protection: slings for trees (abundant), quickdraws for anchors. Rappel device (ATC-style or equivalent). Helmet (mandatory due to rockfall and ice fall hazard). Ice screws (optional, for belayed pitches if team prefers; not typical for this route).
what_to_bring: Insulated jacket (down or synthetic for winter)
Insulated gloves and inner glove liners
Pack (60-70L for two-day, or 35-40L if dayhike push)
Food and water (2-3 liters carrying capacity)
Map and compass (USGS Mount Index quad)
GPS device or smartphone with offline maps
First aid kit (blister treatment, pain relief)
Avalanche beacon, probe, shovel (for group climbing)
pro_tips: Start at 2:30-3:00 AM from the parking lot to maximize daylight on technical sections and descent
Scout the Hourglass Gully entrance from the saddle before committing; if it looks icy and thin, consider bail
On the upper East Ridge, use boot-pack steps for downclimbing if conditions allow; this avoids the need for rappels if snow is stable
Bring a small stove and water bottles; staying hydrated in dry winter air is essential even in cold conditions
Coordinate with a partner or register with local ranger station; rescue from this terrain is expensive and complicated
The Lake Serene trail can be snowy even when lower elevations are clear; microspikes or snowshoes may be necessary for the 4.1-mile approach
Avoid the Hourglass Gully if the upper section shows heavy icefall or hanging ice hazard; rock fall is common from the right (south) side
Practice rappelling before this route; cold hands and gloves make rappel setup slow and error-prone
watch_out: Massive avalanche terrain: the gully and surrounding slopes run thousands of feet; check NWAC avalanche forecast and look for recent slide activity
Icefall: rock and ice regularly shed from the gully's right side; wear helmet always
Exposure: the upper East Ridge has 1,000-foot drops; a fall is fatal; move carefully and use rope for self-belay if nervous
Weather: a clear dawn can turn to storm by afternoon; this area is subject to rapid fog and wind; start early and be willing to bail
Rockfall during descent: loose rocks are common as snow melts; communicate constantly and keep eye on climbers below
backups.pro_needs: Protection is tree-based and natural feature slings; climbers typically clip existing rap slings on descent or place slings around large trees. Rock is granodiorite; belay anchors should be bombproof trees or solid rock features. No bolts; this is entirely natural protection and tree anchors.
backups.best_season: The optimal window is early March through early May, with March-April being ideal for stable snow conditions and solid ice. By mid-May, the gully and upper snow slopes become wet, slushy, and prone to loose rock. Summer (June onward) is not recommended due to exposed wet rock, extensive bushwhacking on the ridge, and extreme difficulty; the gully becomes a steep waterfall with hazardous wet rock. Winter ascents (December-February) are possible but require extreme caution; early-season snows are deep and stable, but temperatures are cold and storms frequent. Spring ascents benefit from consolidated corn snow that hardens overnight, providing the most stable climbing conditions.
backups.approach: Start at the Lake Serene Trailhead and follow Trail #1068 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft of gain to Lake Serene, then traverse talus and boulders around the west side of the lake to its south end. From there head east to a saddle and climb the ridge/gully system southwest of it toward Main Peak, the massif's highest and most technical summit (~5,991 ft). Expect roughly 5,500 ft of total elevation gain, thick brush low on the route, and sustained moderate rock climbing higher up; most parties plan for a 15+ hour car-to-car day or an overnight.
backups.descent_text: The descent mirrors the ascent route but is significantly more technical. On the upper East Ridge, climbers set up two 30-meter rappels using existing rap slings in trees. Descending the Hourglass Gully in spring conditions often involves boot-skiing down 40-50 degree slopes with small wet slides. The steep constriction requires careful down-climbing or short rappels. The ridge traverse back to the lake saddle is exposed with 1,000-foot drops to the northeast side. Return to Lake Serene via the approach slope and descend the 4.1-mile trail by headlamp if a very early start was not made.
backups.bail: Retreat is possible at any point before committing to the Hourglass Gully constriction. If conditions are icy rather than snowy at the gully entrance, turn around and descend via the approach route. If caught in avalanche terrain with unstable snow, descend immediately to the lake saddle. The crux 60-degree pitch on the upper ridge has limited retreat options—do not commit unless conditions and team ability are certain. In whiteout conditions, reverse course before reaching the gully. Avoid descending the gully in deteriorating conditions; retreat to saddle instead.

backups.itinerary: Day 1: Drive from Puget Sound region (1-2 hours) to Lake Serene trailhead. Hike Lake Serene trail (2-3 hours to lake). Camp at Lake Serene if doing this as a two-day climb. Day 2: Early pre-dawn start (2:30 AM typical) from trailhead or 4:30 AM from lake camp. Approach saddle (2-3 hours), climb Hourglass Gully (2-3 hours), traverse East Ridge (1-2 hours), reach summit by mid-morning (8-10 hours from car). Descend via rappels and gully (2-3 hours). Return to Lake Serene (2-3 hours). Hike out (2-3 hours), reaching car by dark. Total single-day push: 15+ hours; two-day with camp: more manageable timing.

climate.fall: Fall (September-November) sees increasing snow, wind, and storms. Not typically climbed due to short daylight, unpredictable weather, and early seasonal storms. Possible light snow cover.
climate.spring: Spring (March-May) is the best climbing season. Snow consolidates into corn, and stable avalanche conditions prevail. Daytime temperatures rise to 25-35°F. May sees increasingly wet conditions and rain-on-snow avalanche hazard. Late spring brings loose rock and wet gully sections.
climate.summer: Summer (June-September) features melted gully sections, exposed wet rock, and severe brush. Avalanche hazard decreases but rockfall increases. Temperatures rise to 45-60°F. Afternoon thunderstorms are common and dangerous on exposed ridge.
climate.winter: Winter (December-February) features deep, stable snow, but extreme cold, high avalanche hazard from new snow, and frequent storms. Temperatures drop to 10-25°F. Days are short (8 hours daylight). Early-season (December-January) snow depth can exceed 10 feet at higher elevations.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate. Orographic lift forces Pacific weather systems upward, creating high precipitation. Temperatures on the peak typically range from 20-35°F in winter, 25-40°F in spring. Wind is frequent and can be extreme, especially on the summit ridge.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: March through April, when a consolidated snowpack buries the ridge brush and corn snow refreezes overnight

May.reason: Early May can still be good, but by mid-month wet slides and rockfall in the gully and melting brush on the ridge take over.

June.reason: The gully turns into wet rock and a waterfall, and the melted-out ridge becomes a steep, brushy fifth-class tree climb.

April.reason: Corn snow that refreezes overnight gives the most secure climbing; start very early before sun loosens the east-facing gully.

March.reason: Consolidated snow buries the brush, the constriction is a snow ramp, and longer days fit the long car-to-car climb.

January.reason: Deep but often unconsolidated snow gives poor axe placements, and frequent storms keep the gully's avalanche paths active.

December.reason: The snowpack may not yet bury the ridge brush, days are very short and storm cycles load the gully's avalanche paths.

February.reason: A deeper snowpack covers the brush and cliffs on the ridge; climb only in a stable spell after a storm cycle settles.

approach_variants.name: Lake Serene Trail #1068, south-end saddle, southwest ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Lake Serene trailhead off Mount Index Road at about 600 ft. Lake Serene Trail #1068 runs about 4.1 miles and 2,000 ft to the north end of the lake, where the trail ends.

Traverse the west side of the lake over talus and huge boulders to the south end. In snow, stay lower, closer to the water — the slope is less steep near the shore. Expect massive avalanche debris on this stretch.

From the south end of the lake head east to the saddle, then take the ridge running southwest from it. That forested ridge is the crux of the approach and the reason this is a spring route: roughly the next 1,000 ft is dense brush and intermittent cliffs, plus one airy ten-foot rock step usually climbed by grabbing roots. Snow cover makes the ridge dramatically easier; bare, it is a fight. Plan on 12+ hours car to car and over 6,000 ft of gain despite the peak being under 6,000 ft.
approach_variants.season: Snow cover — roughly late winter through May; not recommended once melted out
hazards: Steep dense brush and intermittent cliffs on the forested southwest ridge
The airy ten-foot rock step on the ridge, usually climbed on roots
Avalanche debris and avalanche hazard around the lake and in the gully
The wet rock step in the constriction once the gully melts out
Very long day — 12 to 15 hours is normal
approach_variants.baseFinding: Follow the ridge until it runs into the cliffs of Index, then traverse under the cliffs and take the first wide gully on your right. That is the Hourglass. Its shape is the check: it is wide and easy where you enter, constricts high up, then opens again. A gully that is narrow at the point where you step into it is not the one — keep traversing. Once melted out, the constriction holds a large wet rock step; that step is the reason the route is climbed as a snow line rather than in summer, and passing it dry would be mid-to-high fifth on the right side via a short chimney and face, or harder on the left.

bivy.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
bivy.notes: This is the honest awkward centre of the zone. Everything on Mount Index — the Main Peak's north approach, the Hourglass Gully in winter, the North Peak's Northeast Buttress, and the whole Jotunheim cirque with the Norwegian Buttresses — starts from this trailhead at 600 ft and climbs about 2,000 ft in under four miles to the lake at roughly 2,520 ft, then traverses the shore over talus and car-sized boulders to reach the base of the walls in another fifteen or twenty minutes. That is a short, brutal approach rather than a long one, which is exactly why parties overwhelmingly do these routes car-to-car and why there is no camp here. Where a bivy genuinely happens is at the foot of the buttresses, on slab and talus. That spot sits close to the edge of the quarter-mile no-camping ring, probably just outside it but not by a comfortable margin, so sleep as high and as far from the shore as the ground allows and be ready to move if asked. Take a pad and expect rock, not ground. The serious caveat is rockfall: large natural releases have been observed coming off North Index and out of the cleft between the buttresses, so parties are advised to stay low along the lake until they can go straight up to the base — and by the same logic, do not sleep in the fall line of that gully. Winter changes the picture completely: Hourglass Gully is a snow-and-ice objective and the basin is under a deep avalanche-fed snowpack, so a winter bivy here is a snow camp with the walls above you loaded. The day-use hours mean an alpine start is a very early drive from town rather than a walk from a tent.
bivy.water: The lake, and meltwater running off the slabs and the gullies above into midsummer. Later in the season the runnels dry and the lake is the only certainty.
bivy.permit: Read this before planning anything here. Camping and campfires are prohibited within a quarter mile of Lake Serene, and the trailhead itself is signed day use only, open sunrise to sunset, with no overnight parking. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee; a Discover Pass is not valid. So a legal bivy has to be well beyond the lake, out toward the base of the walls, and even then the car is the problem rather than the ground.
bivy.capacity: No established sites at all. What exists is a scatter of flat spots among the boulders and slabs on the south side of the basin, below the walls. Room for a couple of small parties at most, and none of it is comfortable.

gear: ice axe and traction (early season, snow lingers into June)
helmet (mandatory - loose rock and waterfall chimney)
30m rope recommended for the crux waterfall downclimb/optional rappel

backups.overview: Merchant Peak (6,113 ft) is a rugged summit in the Skykomish Mountains above Baring, forming one of the steepest, brushiest walls visible from US-2, alongside neighbors Baring Mountain (1.5 mi south) and Gunn Peak (1.3 mi northwest, the parent peak). It lies within the Wild Sky Wilderness (Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest) and has no built summit trail. The standard South Route leaves the maintained Barclay Lake Trail and climbs the Barclay/Merchant Creek drainage: an off-trail scramble past a sequence of waterfalls (crux around 3,900 ft) into a small alpine basin near 5,200 ft, finishing on class 3 rock via the south slope/east ridge.
backups.beta: From the Barclay Lake Trail, climbers leave the maintained trail at a rocky, Y-shaped creek bed just past the Barclay Creek bridge and follow the drainage upward, bypassing three waterfall steps (left, then right, then a technical squeeze at the third) before breaking out into upper heather meadows and a final rock scramble to the summit block. The rock throughout is exceptionally loose, sandy granodiorite, and route-finding through the upper meadows requires care once the faint climbers' trail fades near the top.
backups.turnaround: Plan for 6-7 hours round trip; since the descent through the loose waterfall gully is hazardous in low light, set a firm early-afternoon turnaround if you haven't reached the crux by then.
backups.rappels: 1-2 rappels in the Waterfall 3 section; optional, as some parties downclimb instead. The fixed anchor there is cord and webbing rather than rings, and a second station is sometimes found at the smaller waterfall below it.
backups.permit: No wilderness permit or quota is required. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
backups.comms: Cell coverage is unreliable in the Barclay Lake/Merchant Peak drainage. Save offline directions before leaving pavement, since app-based driving directions aren't always accurate here.
backups.descent: Reverse the south gully ascent route back to the Barclay Lake Trailhead.

waypoints.name: Barclay Lake Trailhead (FR-6024)
waypoints.note: FR-6024 (Barclay Creek Road) dead-ends here; self-pay day-use fee ($5) or Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: Leave US 2 near Baring and follow FR-6024, the Barclay Creek Road, to where it dead-ends at the Barclay Lake trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or the $5 self-pay day-use fee is required at the kiosk. Barclay Creek runs past the trailhead, so you can top off water here before starting up Barclay Lake Trail #1055 — treat it before drinking.

waypoints.name: Y-shaped creek / gully departure
waypoints.note: Leave the Barclay Lake trail a few hundred feet past the Barclay Creek bridge at this Y-shaped creek fork (not the drainage closer to the lake) to start the south gully scramble.
waypoints.directions: Follow the maintained Barclay Lake Trail #1055 east through old-growth on easy, well-graded tread beside Barclay Creek. The creek mouth you are aiming for has grown in badly; the tell is a faint boot path of piled rocks running a hundred or two hundred feet into the trees to reach the creek bed proper. This is the most commonly missed point on the route, so identify it against a GPS track or a route photo rather than by feel.

waypoints.name: Lower waterfalls (Waterfall 1 & 2)
waypoints.note: First two pour-offs in the gully are bypassed on brushy ledges to the side; footing is loose and slick when wet.
waypoints.directions: From here the drainage is the trail: boulder-hop and scramble straight up the creek bed. The first pour-off is turned on climbers-left on an established boot path; the second is passed by working right toward the cliff band and traversing over the top of the falls. Put helmets on before you start up — the gully is narrow and anything a party above dislodges comes down it.

waypoints.name: Waterfall 3 chockstone crux
waypoints.note: Crux of the route: jammed boulders form a 15-20 ft chimney with small holds on very loose rock over sandy mud; most parties downclimb this same spot on descent.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the gully to where large jammed boulders block it completely. The way through is a Class 3-4 line on climbers-left: a 15-20 ft chimney squeeze on small holds set in loose, sandy rock, with real exposure. Many parties carry a 30m rope for this step even when they intend to downclimb it, and a fixed rap ring has been reported at the top of the falls — treat it as aged gear of unknown condition and back it up with your own natural anchor if you use it.

waypoints.name: Cave feature / gully exit
waypoints.note: A small cave-like rock feature marks where to leave the main gully onto a faint climbers' path through forest and open heather slopes.
waypoints.directions: Above the chockstone the gully eases and opens out into brush and then forest for another 800 ft of gain. Stay in the main drainage the whole way rather than being drawn into side branches, and fix in your mind where you leave it — coming back down into the wrong drainage is the standard descent mistake here.

waypoints.name: Upper alpine meadows/bowl
waypoints.note: Trail fades out in the upper heather meadows; angle climbers' left across talus toward the summit block and final ridge.
waypoints.directions: Pick up the faint climbers' path where it leaves the drainage and follow it up through forest onto open heather, trending climbers-left. It is thin and comes and goes, so treat it as a hint rather than a trail.

waypoints.name: Merchant Peak Summit
waypoints.note: True summit is the northwest high point of the ridge; a lower east peak nearby is commonly mislabeled as Merchant Peak on older maps.
waypoints.directions: Cross the talus out of the bowl and gain the East Ridge, then follow the crest for a final 300 ft or so. The rock here is solid and the scrambling is straightforward Class 3 — a marked change from the loose, sandy ground everywhere below.

backups.detailed_rack: No traditional protection rack is needed for the standard scramble; some parties carry a short rope (around 30m) plus a few slings or rap rings as backup for the crux waterfall/chockstone section, since fixed rap anchors have been reported there.
pro_tips: Carry a 30m rope for the crux waterfall even if you plan to downclimb it.
Start early - round trip commonly takes 6-7 hours car-to-car.
Keep helmets on through the whole gully; parties above can kick down loose rock.
watch_out: Losing the faint boot path where it leaves Barclay Lake Trail at the Y-shaped side creek - identify the landmark carefully or track a GPS route.
The crux waterfall chockstone (~3,900 ft): small holds in loose, sandy-mud rock with real exposure.
Descending the loose gully after dark - budget a full day (parties commonly report 6-7 hours car-to-car).
backups.pro_needs: The route is essentially unprotected scrambling for its entire length; the crux chockstone squeeze has small, unreliable holds on loose, sandy rock where trustworthy gear placements are difficult to find.
backups.approach: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead at the end of FR-6024 (Barclay Creek Road, ~2,280 ft), start up the maintained Barclay Lake Trail #1055 — an easy, well-graded path through old-growth forest paralleling Barclay Creek. After a little over a mile, a few hundred feet past the log bridge that crosses Barclay Creek (roughly 47.792, -121.459), leave the maintained trail; this is well before Barclay Lake itself. Cross toward the base of the south face and pick through brush and talus to locate a Y-shaped side drainage coming down off Merchant Peak (around 47.789, -121.436) — trip reports warn this creek mouth has become overgrown and is easy to walk past; look for a faint boot path of piled rocks leading 100–200 feet into the trees to pick up the creek bed proper. From there the 'trail' is the drainage itself: boulder-hop and scramble directly up the Merchant Creek gully, passing three main waterfall/rock steps. Waterfall 1 is bypassed on climbers-left via an established boot path; Waterfall 2 is passed by working right toward a cliff band and traversing over the top; Waterfall 3 is the crux of the entire approach — a jumble of large, jammed boulders and chockstones with small holds sitting on loose, sandy-mud rock, passed via a line on climbers-left. Above the falls the gully opens into brush, forest, and then heather meadows/slopes (the 'South Slope'); continue up onto the East Ridge for a final ~300 feet of solid, enjoyable Class 3 scrambling to the 6,113 ft summit. Water is available from Barclay Creek at the trailhead and from Merchant Creek throughout the gully (treat before drinking). Hazards include loose rock and rockfall exposure in the gully (helmet strongly recommended, especially with other parties above/below), real route-finding difficulty locating the correct side drainage, the exposed, loose Class 3 moves at Waterfall 3, and lingering snow/avalanche debris in the gully into early summer. Trip reports log roughly 3–4 hours from trailhead to summit.
backups.descent_text: Because this is a scramble rather than a technical rock route, there is no separate rappel-descent line or walk-off trail — nearly all parties reverse the ascent gully (East Ridge to South Slope to South Gully) back down to Barclay Creek and out the Barclay Lake Trail. The crux of the descent is getting back down through the Waterfall 3 chockstone/boulder jam: most parties downclimb it facing in on climbers-left, on the same loose, sandy-mud rock and small holds used on the way up. Some parties choose to rappel this one step instead, particularly in wet conditions or with a less experienced group — trip reports document a single rappel here using a fixed rappel ring at the top of the falls (visible in trip-report photos), backed up with a natural anchor (one party used a nearby log) and the rope run through the ring; a single-strand rappel off a 30m or a doubled 60m rope is more than enough length to clear the drop. Treat that ring as unverified, aged fixed gear rather than a bolted sport anchor, and back it up with your own natural anchor (tree, log, or boulder) if you have any doubt about its condition. Below Waterfall 3, downclimb/scramble past Waterfalls 2 and 1 as ascended, relocate the faint boot path back to the side-drainage junction, and follow it back to the Barclay Lake Trail bridge and out to the trailhead. Descent-specific hazards: rockfall risk is higher going down than up since parties above kick debris onto those below (stay tight as a group or descend one at a time through the gully), the rock in the falls sections gets slick when wet, and it's easy to drop into the wrong side-gully lower down if you don't backtrack carefully to the same drainage used on ascent. Round trip is commonly reported around 6.5–7 hours car-to-car, with the descent taking nearly as long as the ascent (one trip report logged 3.7 hours up and 2.5 hours down).
backups.bail: Below treeline, the only realistic retreat is back down the ascent gully — there is no safer alternate descent once committed above the lower waterfalls. Turn back before entering the crux waterfall section if the party is uncomfortable with loose, essentially unprotectable rock.

pitch_detail.notes: Ascend the creek-bed wash from the trail turnoff; bypass the first waterfall via a use trail on the left.
Work up and right onto the cliffs, passing over the top of the falls.
Large jammed boulders block the gully except for a loose, ~15-20 ft vertical chimney/chockstone squeeze on small holds and sandy rock; fixed rap rings have been reported for the descent.
Faint climbers' trail through heather meadows trending climbers-left, finishing with roughly 300 ft of firmer rock scrambling to the summit.

itinerary.cal: Best done after the snow/waterfall flow drops and the gully dries out, roughly mid-summer through early fall; avoid after rain when the loose rock is wet.

days.note: Standard single-day scramble: hike the Barclay Lake Trail, leave it at the Y-shaped side gully, climb the loose gully past three waterfall steps and the chimney crux, cross the talus/meadow basin, and scramble the class 3 summit block. Descend by reversing the same gully.

access.fees: $5 daily or $30 annual Northwest Forest Pass required to park at Barclay Lake Trailhead (Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid at this USFS fee site).
access.notes: Many of these peaks (Mount Persis, Gunn Peak, Baring Mountain area) sit outside designated wilderness — administratively unrestricted despite serious technical terrain.
access.rules: Wild Sky Wilderness: no permit required for day use; group size capped at 12 people/stock combined; Barclay Lake Trail closed to motorized vehicles, bicycles, and stock; camp only in established sites.
access.landManager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Skykomish Ranger District
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Skykomish Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass required at developed trailheads.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass (or Interagency/America the Beautiful pass)

overnight_permit.what: No overnight permit required; camping is banned within a quarter mile of Lake Serene
overnight_permit.where: A Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park at the Barclay Lake and Lake Serene trailheads. Drive-in campgrounds are reserved on Recreation.gov.

road.name: Forest Road 6024 (Barclay Creek Road)
road.driveNote: From US-2 in Baring (~MP 41-42) turn north onto 635th Place NE/FR-6024 and continue about 4 miles to the Barclay Lake Trailhead. Check current Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts for washouts/closures before driving.

climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate - wet, with heavy wet snow lingering in the shaded gully into June and elevated avalanche potential on approach slopes through early summer; the most reliable snow-free window is August-September.

emergency.nearestHospital: EvergreenHealth Monroe (formerly Valley General Hospital), Monroe, WA

crowds.peakTraffic: weekends in August, when brush and access are driest
crowds.estimatePerSeason: roughly 10-25 scramble parties per season (Barclay Lake approach itself sees far more traffic, but most stop at the lake)

fitnessSpec.hiking: Steep, sustained brush-bashing approach with real elevation gain from the Barclay Lake Trail; expect a long, physically demanding day
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light day-pack (~15-20 lb) — no technical rack needed, but sturdy boots and gaiters for brush recommended

partner_requirements.approachTime: Barclay Lake Trail (a little over a mile) plus a steep, brushy off-trail ascent of the south slopes to the summit; full car-to-car day typically 8-10+ hours
requiredSkills: route-finding through brush and loose terrain with no defined trail
careful movement on loose rock / testing holds before weighting them
basic scrambling downclimb ability (same terrain in reverse)
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Solid Class 3 scrambling experience with comfort on loose, unconsolidated rock; not a beginner objective

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late June through September, with August the single best month

July.reason: Drying out; brush still heavy but slopes are mostly clear of snow

June.reason: Late-season snow can linger on upper slopes and brush is at its thickest/wettest

August.reason: Driest conditions of the year — best footing on loose rock and driest brush

September.reason: Still generally dry, but shortening daylight and increasing chance of early fall weather

weather.typical: Very wet maritime climate overall; the Late June-September window is chosen specifically to avoid that wetness, but afternoon showers are still possible
weather.probability: Occasional afternoon convective showers possible in late summer; brush stays slick and slippery after any rain

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Loose rock and steep brushy slopes create real fall/tumbling-rock hazard; the summit scramble itself is short (roughly the final ~50 ft) with one harder move, but reported to sit on loose rock atop sandy/muddy ground — parties should be cautious of dislodging rock onto others below

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer route (falls within NWAC's Stevens Pass forecast zone in winter/spring, but the route is not climbed in avalanche season)

gaps: No official USFS trail beyond Barclay Lake Trail - the route above the trail is an unofficial boot path/gully scramble with no maintained tread or signage.
Reported rappel anchor (rings) at the crux waterfall is from a single 2011 trip report; current condition/reliability unverified.
Road mileage to the trailhead varies slightly by source (3.9-4.3 mi).
GPS track sourced from public CalTopo map: https://caltopo.com/m/2F1A
