approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead at the end of FR-6024 off US-2 near Baring

backups.rope_note: Most parties climb the crux unroped: a jammed-boulder chimney about 15-20 ft and vertical, in the main canyon. Carry a 30 m rope anyway, because the same step is the crux of the way down. Rather than downclimb it facing in on loose, sandy rock, many parties make one short rappel from the fixed cord and webbing at the top of the falls, and a second station is sometimes found at the smaller waterfall below. Wet conditions or a less experienced group is when that matters. The rock is notoriously loose throughout the canyon, so keep helmets on the whole way.
rack: 30m rope + a few slings/rap rings for the crux waterfall chockstone (optional backup)

approach_variants.name: Barclay Lake Trail to the Y-shaped drainage
approach_variants.notes: Start up the maintained Barclay Lake Trail through old-growth beside the creek — easy, well-graded walking. You leave it after a little over a mile, a few hundred feet past the log bridge over Barclay Creek and well before the lake, then pick through brush and talus toward the base of the south face to find the drainage. From there the drainage IS the route: boulder-hop and scramble straight up the creek bed past three waterfall steps into brush, forest and then upper heather meadows. Water runs in the gully most of the season; treat it before drinking.
hazards: Loose, sandy granodiorite throughout the gully, worst at the crux waterfall
Rockfall from parties above in a narrow drainage
An exposed chockstone squeeze at the third waterfall
Wet snowfields and avalanche debris in the gully into June
High water in the creek bed after heavy rain
approach_variants.baseFinding: Two finds, and the first is the one parties miss. The drainage mouth is a Y-shaped side creek coming down off the peak — not the drainage nearer the lake — and it has grown in badly enough to walk straight past. The tell is a faint boot path of piled rocks running a hundred or two hundred feet into the trees to reach the creek bed proper; identify it against a track or a photograph rather than by feel, because it is the most commonly missed point on the route. Once in the bed you are on the climb. It is punctuated by three waterfall steps that mark your progress: the first is turned on climbers-left on an established boot path, the second by working right toward the cliff band and traversing over the top of the falls, and the third is the crux of the whole outing — large jammed boulders and chockstones blocking the gully completely, passed by a fifteen to twenty foot chimney squeeze on climbers-left, small holds set in loose sandy rock with real exposure. A fixed rappel ring has been reported at the top of that third step; treat it as aged gear of unknown condition and back it up with a tree, log or boulder of your own if you use it. Put helmets on before you start up the bed.

climbing_route.label: South Slope
climbing_route.notes: Above the waterfalls the gully opens into brush, forest, and then heather meadows/slopes — the 'South Slope' — which are followed up toward the East Ridge.

climbing_route.label: East Ridge to the summit
climbing_route.notes: A final ~300 feet of solid, enjoyable Class 3 scrambling on the East Ridge to the 6,113 ft summit.

bivy.name: Money Creek Campground
bivy.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. It sits almost directly under Grotto Mountain and is a sensible base for the Beckler-side objectives, for Baring and the Barclay Creek peaks about fifteen minutes back down the highway, and for anyone wanting a shower-free but civilised night before an early start. Being this low it is usable well outside the alpine season — a real advantage in a zone where several of the objectives are winter routes and everything above 3,000 ft is snowbound. Do not treat it as an approach camp; it is a place to sleep in the valley with a proper toilet and a fire ring, twenty to forty minutes' drive from any of the trailheads.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground. The South Fork Skykomish runs alongside.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee, booked through the federal reservation system or taken first-come at the two unreserved sites. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Fourteen-day stay limit. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire.
bivy.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, most of them accessible. Reservable, with a couple held first-come first-served. Picnic tables, vault toilets, and a swimming hole on the river.

backups.name: Lone Wolf
hazards: Rockfall from loose, largely unweathered rock typical of a newly developed climb.
Rough, pothole- and washout-prone approach road requiring a high-clearance vehicle.
backups.overview: A 2-pitch, 200-ft bolted sport line straight up the main face of The Obelisk, a distinctive pinnacle-like rock embossment protruding from the mountainside in Silver Basin near Snoqualmie Pass.
backups.beta: Lone Wolf follows the obvious, continuous bolt line up The Obelisk's main face for two pitches of 5.10a climbing to bolted chain anchors. It is currently the only documented route on this formation, established in 2020 as part of a small, still-developing crag alongside the neighboring Sofa King Buttress.
backups.turnaround: Because the approach crosses unmaintained talus/scree and a creek with no formal trail, start early enough to reverse the basin approach and the rough forest-road drive before dark, and turn around if weather deteriorates enough to make the loose approach terrain or rock unsafe.
backups.rappels: Lower or rappel from the chain anchors atop each pitch (~30m per pitch); no separate walk-off is documented for this route.
backups.descent: Rappel the route from bolted chain anchors atop each pitch.

waypoints.name: FR-9070 / PCT (#2000) junction near Olallie Meadow, Snoqualmie Pass
waypoints.note: Where FR-9070 crosses the PCT: from I-90 exit 54, Hyak Drive NE becomes FR-9070 and runs 5.4 mi to this crossing. Past the junction, climbers take the left fork of FR-9070 and drive or walk to a large turnaround just below Silver Basin, from which the crag base is a 20-30 min approach on foot. That turnaround has no published name or coordinate, so this junction is the closest fixed reference point rather than the exact parking spot.
waypoints.directions: Leave I-90 at Exit 54 (Hyak) and follow Hyak Drive onto Forest Service Road NF-9070, staying on it past the end of the pavement for about 5.4 miles to the Ollallie Meadow junction where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses the road. Take the left fork of NF-9070 and keep driving until the road ends in a large turnaround just below Silver Basin; that turnaround is where you park, and the pin here marks the PCT crossing rather than the road end itself. The road is not plowed and is generally only clear of snow from about July through November.

waypoints.name: The Obelisk (rock formation/crag), Silver Basin
waypoints.note: Elevation is an estimate from the surrounding terrain (Citidel base area is listed at 4,585 ft; The Obelisk sits further up-slope from the Sofa King Buttress sub-area) — no separate elevation figure is published for this formation.

timing.recommendedStart: Late-morning starts are fine given the short approach; go earlier in peak summer heat.

backups.detailed_rack: A standard sport rack of quickdraws sized for a 2-pitch bolted line; bring enough draws to cover the longer pitch plus the anchor. Bolted chain anchors at the top of each pitch allow rappelling or lowering — no trad gear is needed for protection.
what_to_bring: Sturdy approach shoes for talus/scree and creek crossing
Water — no reliable water source noted at the crag itself
pro_tips: Wear a helmet — the published area description specifically flags sharp, loose rock and falling-rock hazard on this newly developed formation.
This is a very low-traffic, recently bolted crag (FA 2020) with almost no online trip reports or comments — expect to route-find the approach yourself and climb with minimal beta.
watch_out: Loose and sharp rock is characteristic of this new route/area — test holds carefully.
Forest Road NF-9070 is rough with potholes and washouts; a high-clearance vehicle is recommended to reach the road-end turnaround.
No maintained trail beyond the turnaround — the approach crosses scree/talus and a creek crossing.
backups.pro_needs: Fully bolted sport protection throughout; no gear placements required.
backups.best_season: The access road (NF-9070) and basin approach are typically only snow-free from around July through October/November; the road is unplowed and often impassable with snow outside that window, and washouts have made high-clearance vehicles necessary in recent years. As a newly bolted, low-traffic formation (established 2020) with very little online trip-report history, expect variable rock cleanliness and minimal current-conditions beta.
backups.approach: From I-90 Exit 54 (Hyak), follow Hyak Drive onto Forest Service Road NF-9070, continuing past where the pavement ends to the junction at Ollallie Meadow where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses the road. Take the left fork of NF-9070 and follow it until the road terminates in a large turnaround just below Silver Basin. From that turnaround, it's roughly a 20-30 minute approach on foot up into Silver Basin to reach the base of The Citadel's walls, including Sofa King Buttress on the NW side of the basin's east wall. The road is not plowed and is generally only clear of snow from around July through November.
backups.descent_text: From the top of pitch 2, rappel (or lower with a sufficiently long rope) to the bolted chain anchor atop pitch 1, then rappel again to the base of the face. No walk-off descent has been documented for this route.
backups.bail: Retreat is straightforward at any point: lower or rappel from either pitch's bolted chain anchor.

backups.overview: The East Ridge is the easier of Sherpa's two south-side ridge routes: broad blocky terrain and sandy benches at Class 3-4 with only brief low-5th-class steps, passing directly beneath the Sherpa Balanced Rock obelisk before finishing at the true summit. Because it's less sustained than the West Ridge, most parties descend via the West Ridge rather than reversing this line.
backups.beta: From a basin camp around 6,800 ft, follow the east ridge toward the summit; cairns and fixed slings/webbing along the ridge aid route-finding. The route passes around the balanced rock from the north side, which can involve a sketchy traverse over snow or wet rock in early season. The balanced-rock move itself is a shoulder-stand or rope-throw over a pedestal point to gain its east side, then bolt-protected friction climbing to the top, rated 5.7, with a rappel bolt atop.
backups.turnaround: Set an early-afternoon turnaround. If progress over the towers is slow or weather builds, retreat by rappel rather than committing to the upper ridge.
backups.rappels: Descend the West Ridge rap line: 2 single-rope rappels, a scramble, another single, then a double-rope rappel to the west notch (4 total; ~3 combined on two ropes). Parties heading for the South Gully often take only the first 2 and downclimb

backups.permit: Free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead covers both day and overnight trips. Longs Pass and the Ingalls Creek basin lie outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery or quota permit applies.
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage in the Ingalls Creek/Longs Pass basins; the summit ridge may get intermittent signal. A satellite communicator is recommended for this remote wilderness approach.
backups.descent: Descend the west ridge, rappelling the summit block, then the approach slopes.

backups.detailed_rack: A single rack of cams to 2 inches, a set of nuts, plenty of slings for horns, about 8 alpine draws, and a 60m rope for the steps and rappels.

Balanced Rock is a separate ~20-ft obelisk about 100 yards from Sherpa's true summit, not the summit itself — tagging its top requires a shoulder-stand onto the obelisk's east-side pedestal, then a few 5.7 friction moves past an old fixed piton (rappel bolt atop). It's an optional bonus, not required to reach the true summit.
watch_out: Old, sun-bleached fixed slings and a single piton protect the 5.7 Balanced Rock move - inspect before weighting
Route-finding around the Balanced Rock is confusing in poor visibility
Descent is not a reversal of the ascent - know the West Ridge rappels before you commit
backups.pro_needs: The crest offers good crack and horn protection on steeper steps, with run-out moderate sections between. Carry enough slings to protect efficiently over the towers.
backups.best_season: Mid-July through September; the north-facing approach gully can hold snow into early July.
backups.approach: Access is the same Esmeralda Basin/Longs Pass Trailhead used for the West Ridge: follow the Longs Pass Trail (FST 1391) over Longs Pass (~6,200 ft) and down to Ingalls Creek Trail, crossing Ingalls Creek and continuing on the climbers' boot path up into the Sherpa-Argonaut basin (see West Ridge approach for that shared section). From the basin, rather than aiming for the West Ridge notch, angle climber's-left (east), traversing a grassy slope and ascending a talus/scree gully to reach the prominent notch at roughly 8,000 ft, about 600 vertical feet below and east of the true summit. Gain the ridge crest about 100 ft above (east of) the notch via class 2 terrain. This line is longer and more circuitous through loose talus than the direct West Ridge approach, and picking the correct gully/notch is the main route-finding crux; a 50m rope is worth carrying from here since the route above uses fixed rappel slings at several obstacles.
backups.descent_text: Most parties do not reverse the East Ridge; the accepted descent is to finish near the summit, traverse to the top of the West Ridge, and go down using the West Ridge's established rappel line (two single-rope rappels past the crux, a short scramble, another single, then a double-rope rappel to the west notch - see the West Ridge descent for full detail) before dropping back to the basin and Ingalls Creek. Some parties do reverse the East Ridge directly, especially when combining the climb with the nearby Balanced Rock feature: this involves downclimbing/rappelling a vertical chimney using chained-together fixed rappel slings, then a rappel down a steep gully to an exposed slab, then another rappel after crossing the slab, finishing with class 3 downclimbing to the 8,000-ft notch. Expect roughly 2-4 short single-rope rappels off existing (sometimes weathered) fixed slings and chains rather than full ropelength raps; a 50m rope was reported as sufficient. Back up any suspect fixed anchors with your own gear. From the notch/basin, reverse the approach: descend to Ingalls Creek Trail, cross the creek, and climb back over Longs Pass to the trailhead.
backups.bail: Rappels off horns and blocks allow retreat from several points on the ridge, giving a reasonable escape, though the long walk out remains regardless.

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass, then east to the 8,000 ft notch
approach_variants.notes:
The approach shares everything with the West Ridge as far as the basin: Longs Pass Trail from the Esmeralda trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft, down to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft, ford, east on the Ingalls Creek Trail to the Beverly-Turnpike junction, then off-trail up the rib and into the basin beneath Sherpa.

From the basin the two routes diverge. Instead of heading for the West Ridge notch, angle climber's left — east — traversing a grassy slope and then climbing a talus and scree gully toward the notch east of the summit.

This is longer and more circuitous through loose talus than the direct West Ridge line, and picking the right gully is the main problem. There is another level of basin higher and southwest of the summit; ending up in it means you have gone the wrong way. Carry a 50m rope from the notch, since the route above uses fixed slings at several obstacles.
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep; the north-facing approach gully holds snow into early July
hazards: Loose talus and scree in the approach gully
Route-finding: the higher basin southwest of the summit is the overshoot trap
Snow lingering in the north-facing gully into early July
Ingalls Creek ford and the long brushy off-trail section, same as the West Ridge
Fixed slings on the route and on the descent are weathered — carry replacement cord
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The target is a notch at roughly 8,000 ft, east of the true summit and about 600 vertical feet below it. Gaining the ridge crest itself happens about 100 ft above (east of) that notch, on class 2 ground — so the notch is a waypoint, and the crest is gained just past it, not in it.

From the basin the gully leading to it is the obvious one heading up toward that saddle east of the summit, and trip reports confirm that the gully that looks right from below is the right one. The failure mode is overshooting rather than picking the wrong-looking line: parties climb too far and end up in the higher basin to the southwest of the summit.

The orientation check: at the notch the summit should be up and to your west, roughly 600 ft above you. If the summit is above and east, or if you are level with the summit, you are in the wrong saddle.

Sherpa's Balanced Rock sits on the summit ridge and is visible from below — it is the West Ridge's landmark, not this route's start, but it tells you where the summit ridge runs and therefore which way to count from.

Most parties do not reverse this ridge. The accepted descent finishes near the summit, traverses to the top of the West Ridge, and uses that route's rappel line — so plan to end the day on the other side of the peak from where you started climbing.

bivy.name: Sherpa south basin camp
bivy.notes: Sitting a couple of thousand feet above the Ingalls Creek trail in the cirque south of Sherpa, this is where a party wanting a reasonable summit day on the East or West Ridge sleeps. Getting here means leaving the valley trail and grinding up open slopes and gullies with no path to speak of, so the climb from the creek is the crux of the day rather than the ridge. The payoff is that the East Ridge start is an easy morning from here instead of a pre-dawn thrash. It is also the natural base for the Northeast Couloir on Sherpa Balanced Rock, which is reached by continuing up the basin to the notch east of the balanced block. Ground is a mix of scree and low heather and level spots take some hunting; the basin is open and catches wind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams draining the basin are reliable into midsummer and thin out by September; late-season parties should fill on the way up from Ingalls Creek rather than assume
bivy.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, Alpine Lakes Wilderness, outside the Enchantment Permit Area. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, no lottery, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda. No campfires at this elevation, and pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than on the meadow.
bivy.capacity: A small number of established spots on gravel and heather benches; two parties is comfortable, three is crowded

bivy.name: Table Rock bivy, upper Sherpa basin
bivy.notes: A large flat block high in the basin below Sherpa's south side, used by parties who want the East Ridge to start within minutes of waking rather than an hour and a half above camp. From here the route climbs a broad gully trending north-northeast to gain the crest east of the balanced rock, then follows blocks and sandy benches west past the block to the summit. It is exposed, windy and cold compared with the basin camp a thousand feet lower, and whether the extra height is worth carrying water up for is a real judgement call rather than an obvious yes. Anyone attempting Sherpa Balanced Rock's Northeast Couloir gets the most from this position, since the couloir tops out close by. Leave no trace of a platform; the rock is bare and the ground around it is fragile.
bivy.water: None dependable. Snow patches persist into midsummer and can be melted, but treat it as a dry bivy and carry water up from the basin below.
bivy.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, no Enchantment lottery involved. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda if you came over Longs Pass. No fires, and nothing here to build one with.
bivy.capacity: Two to four people on flat rock; this is a perch rather than a campsite, and there is nothing else level nearby

bivy.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
bivy.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely outside the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
bivy.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

bivy.name: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
bivy.notes: This is the base for the south side of both Argonaut and Sherpa, and it is what makes those peaks feasible as overnights rather than brutal single pushes. Two ways in. From Esmeralda you climb to Longs Pass at about 6,200 feet and drop roughly 1,400 feet to the valley, then walk east along the trail until you are under your peak; Sherpa's south basin is about a mile down, Argonaut's exit gully perhaps three. From the low trailhead off US 97 you walk in flat but far, upwards of ten miles to reach the same ground, which trades the pass for distance and suits a party with time. A third link comes over Fourth Creek from the Beverly Creek trailhead in the Teanaway and requires fording Ingalls Creek, which is genuinely dangerous in June. The valley is low and sheltered, so it is buggy through midsummer and warm at night, and the brush between the trail and the open slopes above is the real work of the approach. Sites are dispersed rather than built, so pick an existing one instead of clearing new ground. The elevation of the trail changes across the several miles covered here, so no single figure is given.
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs strongly all season and side streams come in from the north wall; the only dry stretch is the climb over Longs Pass, which carries no water at all in either direction
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness under the Cle Elum Ranger District, entirely outside the Enchantment Permit Area. A free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, there is no lottery, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is needed to park at Esmeralda; the low Ingalls Creek trailhead off US 97 has its own parking requirement. Campfires are restricted seasonally and are a poor idea in any case; the valley is dry and forested. Camp at least 200 feet from the creek.
bivy.capacity: Numerous flat, well-used sites strung along several miles of valley floor and its side creeks; there is no quota and no realistic crowding, so a party can nearly always find its own ground

backups.overview: A single-pitch alpine granite route featuring smearing and jug climbing on solid granite near Lake Viviane, accessible as top-rope or traditional lead.
backups.beta: The route starts with a layback and smears before mantling onto a ledge. The crux is a 5.10ish move through a thin crack. Short climbers may have a harder time due to the length and reach required. Can be set as top-rope using a boulder at the top.
backups.turnaround: Given the alpine location and weather exposure, climbers should plan to start climbing early (dawn) and aim to be off the rock by early afternoon to avoid afternoon thunderstorms. If weather deteriorates or parties are delayed, be prepared to bivy near the route or descend via the trail.
backups.permit: Enchantment permit area: overnight stays May 15-Oct 31 require a quota permit (Recreation.gov advance lottery); day trips need the free self-issued day-use permit at the trailhead.
backups.comms: Cell service is unreliable in the Enchantments basin due to remote alpine location and surrounding granite. No reliable cell coverage should be assumed. Satellite messengers or personal locator beacons (PLBs) are recommended for emergency communication. The nearest ranger station is at Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest headquarters in Wenatchee.
backups.descent: Downclimb or rappel from the anchors/boulder at the top (typically short rappel to ground level given the 30 ft length).

backups.detailed_rack: #2 carabiners, #2 and small stoppers for lead protection. For top-rope setup: two 60m ropes or two shorter ropes (single rope climbing via natural anchor). Quickdraws for leading. Helmet required.
what_to_bring: sleeping bag (rated for potential sub-freezing nights)
fire starter or lighter (for stove use only)
pro_tips: Start climbing at first light to minimize afternoon thunderstorm exposure; be off the rock by 1-2 PM
Short climbers may find success using better footwork on the smear section rather than relying on reach; work the techniques rather than power
The boulder anchor at top is solid granite; test all holds before weighting
Set up top-rope early in the day to allow multiple ascents without leading repeatedly
The route is short but compact; the crux is well-protected if solid rock is used for placements
watch_out: Do not attempt to climb late in the day due to thunderstorm risk and fading light at alpine elevation
Descending in darkness on the trail from Viviane is hazardous; headlamps and navigation skills essential
Early season (May-June): Snow and avalanche danger on the steep approach above Upper Snow Lake make route inaccessible; wait for conditions to stabilize
Afternoon weather deterioration can be rapid; if weather changes suddenly, descend immediately rather than waiting out conditions on the route
backups.pro_needs: Light traditional pro: #2 carabiners and small stoppers are sufficient for the thin crack crux. The route does not require extensive rack; a single set of small to mid-sized cams could supplement protection on the crux if desired. Most climbers use top-rope given the short length and natural anchor at top.
backups.best_season: July through August offers the most stable alpine weather in the Enchantments, with minimal snow at lake level. September and early October are viable shoulder months but expect cooler temperatures and potential early season snow higher up. May-June and late October are not recommended due to significant snow accumulation, avalanche hazard on the steep approach above Upper Snow Lake, and permit restrictions.
backups.descent_text: Since this is a short 30-foot route, climbers can either carefully downclimb the same line or set up a short rappel from the boulder anchor at the summit of the route. A single 30-60m rope is sufficient. Alternatively, walk off if setting up as a top-rope via the boulder.
backups.bail: From the crux position, downclimbers can retreat by downclimbing through the thin crack section and mantling back to the ledge, then retracing the initial layback/smear section. The route is short enough that bail is straightforward. In emergency, rappel from the top anchor.

pitch_detail.notes: Single 30-foot pitch starting with a layback and smearing sequence, transitioning to a mantle onto a ledge. Crux is located in the upper third: a 5.10ish move through a thin crack requiring precise footwork and hand placement. Well-protected with small traditional gear (#2 cams, stoppers). Finish on solid ground near a large boulder suitable for anchoring.

backups.itinerary: Day 1: Hike from Snow Lakes Trailhead to Lake Viviane (6-8 hours with full pack). Establish camp at Viviane Campsite. Day 2: Acclimatization day; scout the route and set up top-rope if desired. Day 3: Climb Smears, Jugs, and Rock & Roll (1-2 hours of climbing). Day 4: Descent to trailhead (5-6 hours).

access.notes: 2026 lottery application window Feb 15–Mar 1 (results after Mar 17, accept/pay by Mar 31). ~25% of overnight slots also released as a walk-up daily lottery the day before entry. Season requiring the overnight permit: May 15–Oct 31. A single-day ascent with no camp inside the boundary never needs the lottery.
access.rules: Overnight groups inside the permit boundary capped at 8 people, must camp together at one previously-impacted site, max 14 consecutive days, no re-entry same trip, permits non-transferable. Bear-resistant food storage mandatory forest-wide.
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — Alpine Lakes Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Stuart Lake, Eightmile, and Snow Lakes trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (overnight permit holders get a covering parking pass instead).

road.name: Snow Lakes Trailhead, Icicle Creek Road, Leavenworth
road.status: Paved Icicle Road for 4.2 miles from US-2 to the trailhead; a long maintained trail leads into the Enchantments core.
road.driveNote: Roughly 2.5-3 hours from Seattle via US-2/US-97 to Leavenworth then Icicle Creek Road.
road.seasonalGate: Not gated at the Snow Lakes Trailhead itself, but the Icicle Creek drainage has been subject to temporary Forest Service closures (e.g., camping restrictions, and a 2025 emergency closure during an active law-enforcement search)

climate.fall: September-early October: Temperatures dropping (45-60 F day, 25-35 F night). Morning frost common. Increasing storm frequency. Late October: Significant weather deterioration, early snow possible at higher elevations above 7,000 feet.
climate.spring: Snow present at lake level through mid-June in most years. Cold temperatures (freezing at night, 30-40 F during day). Avalanche danger on the steep approach above Upper Snow Lake. Not recommended for climbing.
climate.summer: Best and most stable season (July-August). Daytime temperatures 55-70 F, nights 35-45 F. Low precipitation, clear skies common. Occasional afternoon thunderstorms. Ideal climbing window.
climate.winter: Deep snow and avalanche terrain make the basin a winter travel/ski objective only — not accessible for rock climbing.
climate.typical: Alpine environment with rapid weather changes. Temperatures range from 40-65 F during summer days, dropping to 20-40 F at night. Wind is common at altitude. Afternoon thunderstorms develop frequently June-September.
climate.forecastZone: NOAA Forecast Zone: Central Washington Cascades (Leavenworth area)

emergency.notes: Cell service unreliable in Enchantments; sat phones or PLBs recommended. Rescue from alpine location will be helicopter-assisted given remote terrain and steep approach. Self-rescue and preventive measures are essential. Nearest Ranger Patrol typically based out of Wenatchee; response times can be several hours.
emergency.rangerStation: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee Ranger District (main office in Wenatchee; patrol rangers may contact via emergency channels)
emergency.nearestHospital: Cascade Medical Center, 817 Commercial Street, Leavenworth, WA 98826. Phone: (509) 548-5815. 24-hour Emergency Department. Approximate drive time from Snow Lakes Trailhead: 45-60 minutes (hike down plus drive).
